extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112, first paragraph), including how to analyze species vs. genus claims, examiner burden, and how to handle applicant replies and claim amendments. Focused on examination practice and determining entitlement to earlier filing/priority dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession of the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must show that applicant was in possession of the claimed invention; the disclosure must be 'full, clear, concise, and exact' so that a skilled artisan recognizes applicant had the invention as claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a complete structure is disclosed, the written description requirement is satisfied for that species or embodiment. The inquiry is factual and considers whether the disclosure conveys with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that applicant was in possession of the invention as of the filing date (Vas-Cath, Ralston Purina, Lockwood citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete structure disclosure satisfies species support
rubrics_metrics.description: When the application as filed discloses the complete structure (or acts of a process) of the claimed invention as a whole, the written description requirement is satisfied for that species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112, first paragraph) for lack of written description should be made for that species if complete structure is disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function plus minimal structure with established structure-function correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: In arts with a well-established correlation between structure and function (e.g., biotech), disclosure of function plus minimal structural identifying characteristics may satisfy the written description requirement because a skilled artisan could predict structure from function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when a strong correlation exists, one skilled in the art can predict structure from function with reasonable confidence; but this depends on maturity and predictability of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-only disclosure is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of function alone (without adequate identifying characteristics or structure) is generally insufficient to satisfy the written description requirement and is 'little more than a wish for possession.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases (Eli Lilly, In re Wilder) show that mere statement of a desired result or goal without enabling identification of how to achieve it fails the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in determining possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession is assessed by considering multiple factors rather than a single test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical/chemical properties, functional characteristics (esp. if coupled with known/disclosed structure-function correlation), and the method of making the claimed invention. Any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguishes the claimed invention from other materials and leads one of skill to conclude possession may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater disclosure required in unpredictable/emerging arts
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions in unpredictable or emerging technologies, more evidence in the specification is required to show possession than in mature, predictable arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of only a method of making plus function may not support claims (e.g., product-by-process) in unpredictable arts; reduction to practice or more detailed structure may be needed (Fiers, Amgen, Burroughs Wellcome).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims: need clarity that process produces product
rubrics_metrics.description: A product-by-process claim is supported when the specification shows the process actually produces the product or otherwise evidences possession of the product; mere process description or product characterization may be insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the acts set forth cannot be shown to be performable or to produce the product, the written description may fail. When the process has actually been used to produce the product, written description for the product-by-process claim is clearly satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization alone may be insufficient to show possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing only properties or characterization of a product without enabling or structural disclosure may fail to evidence possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court precedent (Amgen) explains that conception of complex chemical compounds requires ability to define and distinguish the compound structurally or by method of preparation, not solely by a principal biological property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claims require representative number of species
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to a genus may be supported by disclosure of a 'representative number of species' that are adequately described and are representative of the entire genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When substantial variation exists within the genus, a sufficient variety of species must be described to reflect that variation; failure to disclose representative species requires rejection for lack of written description (AbbVie example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single species may support genus in some circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of only one species can support a claim to a genus only if the disclosure indicates the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus or when a skilled artisan would understand the genus is contemplated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include situations where the specification makes clear the invention is not limited to the particular species disclosed (Rasmussen, In re Herschler, In re Smythe). Courts caution, however, that unpredictability in the art may prevent a single-species disclosure from being representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure must reasonably convey the inventor had possession of the later-claimed subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The dispositive test is whether the disclosure 'reasonably conveys to the artisan that the inventor had possession at that time of the later claimed subject matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective standard per Gosteli/Vas-Cath; possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, reduction to practice, or 'ready for patenting' disclosures such as drawings or structural chemical formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification need not use claim terms verbatim
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter need not be described in the exact terminology of the claim to satisfy the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if a claim amendment introduces limitations not present in the original disclosure (departure/addition/deletion), the examiner should conclude the subject matter is not described and reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or deny benefit of the earlier filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each claim limitation must be supported in the original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with written description (or to be entitled to an earlier filing/priority date), each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an explicit limitation is not present, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at filing that the description requires that limitation (Hyatt v. Boone). Inherency requires that missing matter is necessarily present and recognized by persons of ordinary skill; probabilities or possibilities are insufficient (In re Robertson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements described as essential must be claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the originally filed disclosure identifies elements as essential or critical, those elements must be included in any claim directed to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to claim elements described as essential can result in rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or denial of priority/benefit (Johnson Worldwide, Gentry Gallery, Tronzo citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner burden to rebut presumption of adequate written description
rubrics_metrics.description: A description as filed is presumed adequate; the examiner has the initial burden to present evidence/reasoning by a preponderance to explain why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the claimed invention in the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must have a reasonable basis for challenge and, when rejecting, must set forth express factual findings supporting the lack of written description (Wertheim, In re Marzocchi). A general allegation of 'unpredictability' is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection content requirements: identify limitations and establish prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner should (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue and (B) establish a prima facie case with reasons why a person skilled in the art would not have recognized possession in view of the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple statement pointing out where support is not apparent may suffice when applicable; examiners should suggest claim amendments that can be supported by the original disclosure, being mindful not to introduce new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling applicant reply: reassess in view of the whole record
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon applicant reply, the examiner must reconsider the written description analysis in view of the entire record (amendments, arguments, evidence). If the record now shows adequacy, do not repeat the rejection; otherwise repeat with full response to rebuttal and analyze any affidavits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits or evidence submitted must be thoroughly analyzed and discussed; do not maintain a rejection if the record as a whole cures the defect (In re Alton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete patentability determination before imposing rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must complete the patentability determination under all relevant statutory provisions (35 U.S.C. 101, 112, 102, 103) and confirm correctness of proposed rejections before issuing an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office actions should clearly communicate findings, conclusions, and bases, and when possible offer helpful suggestions on how to overcome rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-(or step-)plus-function limitations require corresponding structure/materials/acts disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation expressed in means- or step-plus-function language must be supported by disclosure of corresponding structure, material, or acts in the specification; absent such disclosure the limitation is indefinite and also lacks adequate written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph), the claim covers the corresponding structure and equivalents. If the specification fails to disclose sufficient corresponding structure that performs the entire function, the limitation is indefinite (In re Donaldson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments and new claims must be supported by original disclosure for priority/benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: New or amended claims (or claims asserting entitlement to an earlier filing/priority date under 35 U.S.C. 119/120/365/386) must be supported by the original disclosure as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant should specifically point out the support for amendments; examiner's initial burden applies. Lack of support requires rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or denial of benefit of the earlier filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical circumstances giving rise to written description issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description issues commonly arise on claim amendments, reliance on parent filing date (35 U.S.C. 120), reliance on foreign/provisional priority (35 U.S.C. 119), interference counts, original claims that are functionally defined or broad genera, and indefiniteness of means-plus-function limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to these contexts and apply the same description analysis. For interference/priority contexts, the earlier application must meet the written description requirement for the subject matter of the count or claimed priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative disclosure may rely on known art or inventor description for structure-function correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: A representative number of species or a structure-function correlation sufficient to support a genus may be established either by disclosure in the specification or by knowledge known in the art at the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: disclosure of an amino acid sequence may be sufficient to convey possession of the genus of nucleic acids encoding it because the genetic code is widely known (In re Bell, In re Baird); conversely, lack of representativeness (only one structurally similar antibody) may fail (AbbVie).
